opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing I emphasize most is that students should really build things end to end. Machine-learning systems is a field where you can't just sit at the level of ideas. You have to touch the whole stack, from the model and the algorithms down to the compiler, the runtime, and sometimes the hardware. A lot of the most interesting insights only show up when you actually try to make something work in practice and you hit a real bottleneck.

So I encourage my students to get their hands dirty early. Write the code, make it run, measure it, and then ask why it's slow or why it breaks. That loop of building, measuring, and understanding is where good research questions come from. Many of the projects I've been involved in, like XGBoost or TVM, didn't start as a grand plan. They started because there was a concrete problem we wanted to solve, and we kept pushing on it.

The second thing is open source and community. I tell students that research doesn't end when the paper is accepted. If you build something real and put it out there, people will use it in ways you never expected, and that feedback makes your work much better. It also teaches you to care about usability, engineering quality, and how your system fits into a bigger ecosystem. Those are skills that matter whether you go into academia or industry.

Finally, I try to give students a lot of freedom to find what they're passionate about. My job is less about handing out problems and more about helping them pick problems that are both important and that they genuinely enjoy. When a student really cares about a problem, they'll go deep and stick with it through the hard parts, and that persistence is usually what turns a good idea into real impact.

r001.rationale: The response discusses open source, community feedback, and building across the software stack, but it does not state that adoption requires collaboration across the team.

r002.rationale: The response encourages students to build and release real systems that people can use, but does not identify creating opportunities for students to carry research projects through to adoption as an advising goal.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The first thing I emphasize is that machine-learning systems is really a field at the intersection of two things that move fast at the same time: the models and algorithms on one side, and the hardware and systems on the other. So I tell students early on that they can't just be a systems person or just a machine-learning person. They have to build enough depth in both to see where the interesting problems actually are, because the best problems usually sit right at the boundary, where an algorithmic change makes something possible on the hardware, or a hardware constraint forces you to rethink the algorithm.

The second thing is to build real things and put them in front of real users. A lot of my own work, XGBoost, TVM, MLC LLM, started as something we needed ourselves, and then the feedback from people actually using it shaped the research direction more than any paper reading would have. So I encourage students to open-source their work, to care about the engineering, to make the code something other people can build on. That feedback loop is one of the fastest ways to learn what matters versus what just looks good on a benchmark.

The third thing is choosing problems with some ambition, and being comfortable that the first version is going to be rough. I'd rather a student pick a direction where, if it works, it changes how people do things, and then we iterate on it, than optimize for a safe incremental result. That requires some patience from both of us, because the payoff isn't immediate.

And finally, I try to stay hands-on. I still write code, I still look at the kernels and the compiler passes with students, because I think in systems research the details are where the insight is. You can't advise well from a distance in this area. So the goal is really to work alongside students rather than just direct them, and over time they take ownership and start setting the direction themselves. That's when I know it's working.

astra-6.text:
I emphasize helping students develop their own judgment about what problems are worth working on. In machine-learning systems, it’s easy to start with a technique and look for somewhere to apply it. I encourage students to start with a concrete need: What is holding people back, and why don’t existing approaches solve it well?

Then the goal is to connect ideas with building. Implementing a system and seeing how it behaves can challenge your assumptions and lead to better research questions. As an advisor, I want to provide enough guidance to help students make progress, while giving them room to take ownership and become independent researchers.

sol-6.1.text:
I emphasize helping students develop their own judgment. In machine-learning systems, it’s easy to start with a technique or an optimization, but I encourage students to ask: What problem are we solving? Why does it matter? And what experiment would tell us whether our idea actually helps?

I also encourage them to build things and learn from what happens. Implementing an idea often reveals assumptions that weren’t obvious on paper. My role as an advisor is to help students ask sharper questions and gradually take ownership of the research, so they become independent researchers.
